canonical_topic: Roles in a deregulated electricity grid
definition: In deregulated power markets, the generation, transmission, and retail-sales functions of the grid are split among separate companies rather than being bundled into one utility.
core_idea: Deregulation unbundles the electricity supply chain into distinct roles: a merchant generator that sells power (usually to a load-serving entity), a wires-only investor-owned utility that owns transmission/distribution but not generation, a load-serving entity (LSE) that acts as intermediary between the grid operator, generators, and consumers, and a provider of last resort (POLR) that is obligated to serve customers who haven't chosen a supplier or whose supplier has failed.
key_points: Merchant generator: sells power to another company, typically a load-serving entity, rather than directly to end-users.
Investor-owned (wires) utility: owns transmission infrastructure but not generation assets.
Load-serving entity (LSE): intermediary providing electric service to end-users or wholesale customers.
Provider of last resort (POLR): the LSE obligated to supply consumers who don't pick a supplier or whose chosen supplier goes out of business.
relationships: Contrasts with the bundled roles found in regulated (integrated utility) markets.
trading_implications: Merchant generators are the natural counterparties for physical/financial power sales, since they don't have their own captive retail load.
caveats: The 'wires' utility owning transmission does not mean it also owns or dispatches generation in a deregulated market.
